taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO (2026 backbone) accepts Yucca torreyi as a distinct species and cites the 2025 Phytotaxa Yucca phylogeny. Flora of North America (2002) instead included it within Yucca treculeana/treculiana, so older sources and labels may conflict.
look_here_first: First decide whether you have a tree yucca with fleshy fruit. If yes, look for Torrey’s traditional field combination: rigid spear-like leaves with marginal threads, the leaf tip portion often rolled inward, versus the mostly non-threaded, non-inrolled leaves of Trecul’s yucca.
project_tracker_diagnostic: arborescent/tree-like yucca with a trunk and crown of rigid dagger leaves; leaves commonly with marginal threads in the traditional Texas field key; apical leaf portion often inrolled so margins approach each other; traditional key gives a relatively slender ovary, not over about 7 mm diameter at flowering; flowers cream to whitish, often in a dense panicle; fruit fleshy, indehiscent, berry-like rather than a dry splitting capsule

project_inclusion.range_basis: Burnet — Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas records Yucca torreyi from Burnet County; contemporary field documentation also records flowering plants at Longhorn Cavern State Park, Burnet County. Bexar — Government Canyon State Natural Area vegetation documentation for Bexar County includes Yucca torreyi among local succulents. Val Verde — Amistad National Recreation Area vascular-plant inventory in Val Verde County lists Yucca torreyi; Lower Pecos sources likewise describe it as a common yucca of the study area.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Yucca treculiana: This is the critical pair. Traditional Texas keys use marginal threads + inrolled leaf tips + a slender ovary for Y. torreyi, versus mostly non-threaded, non-inrolled leaves + a stouter 7–12 mm ovary for Y. treculiana. Geographic context and fruit/flower details should be used because historical lumping and possible hybridization make leaf-only IDs risky. Yucca rupicola: Both may occur on the Edwards Plateau, but Y. torreyi is trunk-forming with rigid dagger leaves and fleshy fruit; Y. rupicola stays low/trunkless with flexible twisted leaves and a dry dehiscent capsule.
